analysis.one_liner: Raises penalties on tax shelter promoters and closes offshore tax haven loopholes.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2004 with one cosponsor, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have cracked down on two things: tax shelters sold to corporations and wealthy individuals, and the use of offshore tax havens that keep their records secret from U.S. tax authorities. It would have raised fines on the accounting, law, and financial firms that design and sell these schemes, required them to keep client lists the IRS can inspect, banned advisors from getting paid a share of the tax they help clients avoid, and forced Americans to report large payments to countries on an annual Treasury list of uncooperative tax havens — with denied tax benefits for income routed through them. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received any vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers who pay what they owe. Abusive shelters and offshore havens let a small set of corporations and wealthy individuals shift their tax burden onto everyone else — either the revenue must be made up from other taxpayers, or services are cut, or debt grows. The bill would also help honest accounting and law professionals by imposing the same opinion standards on every advisor, and help investors and employees at companies whose financial statements were propped up by shelter-driven tax positions, since penalty disclosures would have to appear in SEC filings.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary taxpayers who pay their share

how_it_helps.text: It would raise penalties on promoters of abusive tax shelters to as much as 150 percent of the income they derive from the activity, and make those penalties and settlement payments non-deductible as a business expense [S2][S3].

It would impose a 40 percent penalty on understated tax from transactions lacking economic substance — deals with no real business purpose beyond reducing tax — reduced to 20 percent if the taxpayer disclosed the transaction [S3].

It would require United States persons to report transfers of $10,000 or more to jurisdictions on an annual Treasury list of uncooperative tax havens, deny foreign tax credits and defer tax benefits on income from those havens, and penalize non-reporting by 20 percent of the transfer [S2][S3].

It would let Treasury share tax return information with the SEC and banking regulators for shelter and fraud investigations, ban tax advisors from collecting fees contingent on projected tax savings, and express the Senate's sense that more IRS enforcement money go toward shelters used by corporations and high-net-worth individuals [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Accounting, law, and financial firms that design, sell, and give opinions on tax shelters — penalties up to 150 percent of their shelter income, new client-list and disclosure duties, and a ban on fees tied to projected tax savings. Corporations and wealthy individuals who used shelters or parked income in secrecy jurisdictions would face a 40 percent penalty on no-substance deals, loss of foreign tax credits and deferral benefits for income in listed havens, and new reporting duties on transfers of $10,000 or more to those countries. Some compliance cost would spill onto businesses and individuals with legitimate cross-border dealings in listed havens.

drawbacks.text: The bill would require United States persons to report transfers of $10,000 or more to any jurisdiction Treasury lists as an uncooperative tax haven, with a penalty of 20 percent of the transfer for failure to report — a burden that would fall on legitimate cross-border businesses and individuals, not only shelter users [S3].

The bill would let the Internal Revenue Service Commissioner rescind certain shelter penalties in his sole discretion, with no administrative or judicial review of that determination, concentrating significant enforcement judgment in one office [S3].

Banning fees contingent on tax savings and imposing opinion standards would raise the cost of sophisticated tax advice across the board, including for taxpayers with defensible planning questions, and would push some planning work further offshore or underground [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On the helping side, the bill aimed at a real and large problem: tax shelters and offshore havens shift the tax burden onto employees and small businesses that cannot afford promoters and haven structures, and stiffer penalties plus information sharing with the SEC and banking regulators [S2][S3] would have made the schemes riskier to sell. On the cost side, the burden would fall partly on legitimate activity: reporting every transfer of $10,000 or more to listed havens, and a 20 percent penalty for failing to do so [S3], would add paperwork for ordinary cross-border business and personal transfers, and Treasury's annual haven list would carry real consequences for jurisdictions and firms with limited warning. The bill also gave the Commissioner sole, unappealable discretion to rescind certain penalties [S3], a trade of due process for enforcement flexibility that a careful drafter would revisit. And the contingent-fee ban [S2], while aimed at shelter sales, could make even defensible tax advice more expensive. The costs are real but manageable; the bill's main weakness is that it never got any scrutiny at all — no hearings, no markups, no amendments — so the public never saw the trade-offs weighed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 12, 2004, read twice, and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance [S5].
The action history records no further steps — no hearings, no committee vote, no floor action — after the referral [S5].
The 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, without the bill receiving a vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firms that promoted tax shelters and the corporations and wealthy individuals who used them, along with offshore secrecy jurisdictions — none faced the new penalties, disclosure rules, or benefit denials the bill would have imposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Shelter promoters and offshore haven users

for.name: Sen. Carl Levin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Michigan; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Tax Shelter and Tax Haven Reform Act on March 12, 2004 and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor [S5].

for.name: Sen. Norm Coleman
for.role: U.S. Senator from Minnesota; sole cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it a bipartisan introduction [S4].

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on March 12, 2004 and took no further action on it — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — for the rest of the 108th Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Democrat (Levin) with one Republican cosponsor (Coleman) [S4], and no party bloc ever took a recorded position because no vote was ever held.

industries.industry: Accounting firms that design and sell tax shelters
industries.note: Penalties for promoting shelters could reach 150 percent of promoter income, fees contingent on tax savings would be banned, and written shelter advice would face new standards, plus information sharing with the SEC and audit regulators [S2][S3]. The bill died, so none of this took effect.

industries.industry: Law and financial firms promoting or advising on shelters
industries.note: The bill would expand injunctions against promoters, strip confidentiality for shelter communications, and penalize aiding and abetting understated tax at up to 150 percent of the advice-derived income [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Corporations and high-net-worth individuals using shelters and havens
industries.note: Economic-substance rules and a 40 percent penalty on no-substance transactions, plus denied tax benefits for income in listed havens, would raise the expected cost of aggressive avoidance toward or above the tax saved [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Banks and financial institutions in secrecy jurisdictions
industries.note: Mandatory reporting of $10,000-plus transfers and an annual Treasury list of uncooperative havens would make offshore structures in those jurisdictions harder to use and easier to trace [S2][S3].
